title: THE SAMARITAN WOMAN HAD FIVE HUSBANDS—AND JESUS ALREADY KNEW
paragraphs:
THE SAMARITAN WOMAN HAD FIVE HUSBANDS—AND JESUS ALREADY KNEW
She came to the well carrying a water jar. Jesus was waiting for the part of her life she couldn't hide.
What if Jesus sat down beside you today…

and before you could explain yourself, defend yourself, clean up the story, delete the messages, blame what happened, blame who hurt you, or carefully choose the version of your life you wanted Him to hear…
Every promise you made to God and quietly broke.
Every place you keep returning to because, for a few moments, it makes the thirst disappear.
Because one afternoon in Samaria, a woman walked toward a well expecting nothing more than water.
She had no idea she was walking toward Someone who knew her entire story.
John tells us that Jesus came to a Samaritan town called Sychar and sat beside Jacob's well, tired from the journey. A Samaritan woman came to draw water, and Jesus did something startlingly simple.
The conversation immediately crossed boundaries. She herself recognized how unusual it was that a Jewish man was speaking to a Samaritan woman.
But Jesus had not come merely to discuss water.
He began speaking about something deeper.
A gift that would reach a thirst no earthly well could satisfy.
Then Jesus said something that changed the temperature of the entire conversation.
“Go, call thy husband, and come hither.” — John 4:16, KJV
It is the silence that happens when God touches the one subject you hoped the sermon would avoid.
But Jesus already knew the rest.
In the Greek text of John 4:18, the words are painfully direct:
“καὶ νῦν ὃν ἔχεις οὐκ ἔστιν σου ἀνήρ”
And the one she had now was not her husband.
And now another man who was not her husband.
And perhaps the most breathtaking part of the story is this:
He had already offered her living water.
Jesus did not discover her history halfway through the conversation and suddenly reconsider His offer.
He knew before He asked for a drink.
He knew before He talked about eternal life.
He knew what was behind the carefully chosen words, “I have no husband.”
Still He led her toward truth.
Still He revealed Himself to her.
But don't turn grace into sentimental permission to remain unchanged.
Jesus did not pretend her situation was something it wasn't.
Biblical grace does not require Jesus to become comfortable with our darkness.
Biblical grace brings us into His light.
And we need to be careful here, because Christians have sometimes preached details about this woman that John never gives us.
The Bible does not say she was a prostitute.
It does not tell us that all five marriages ended because she was sexually immoral.
It does not tell us whether she had been divorced, abandoned, widowed, mistreated, or whether different circumstances surrounded different marriages.
We are not allowed to manufacture sins Scripture does not accuse her of committing.
What Scripture does tell us is enough.
The man she presently had was not her husband.
That is where the story becomes uncomfortable for us.
Because maybe you don't have five husbands.
Maybe your well has another name.
A relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
The desperate need to be admired.
The hidden hunger to be wanted.
The endless scrolling because silence makes you face yourself.
Maybe everybody thinks you're doing wonderfully.
Maybe you post Scripture while privately losing the battle.
Maybe you worship on Sunday and spend Monday running back toward the same well.
One more person telling me I'm attractive.
But Jesus told the woman something every thirsty soul eventually discovers:
“Whosoever drinketh of this water shall thirst again.” — John 4:13, KJV
Because sin always sends you back thirsty.
Human approval sends you back thirsty.
Success eventually sends you back thirsty.
The person you thought would complete you eventually reveals that no human being was created to occupy the throne of your soul.
We keep lowering our buckets into wells that cannot save us.
“Whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst.” — John 4:14, KJV
He wasn't giving her a religious technique for becoming a more impressive version of herself.
And eventually this conversation moved from her relationship history to worship, truth, and Messiah.
She told Him that she knew Messiah was coming.
Then came one of the most staggering moments in the chapter.
The woman who walked to the well carrying an ordinary jar found herself speaking with the Christ.
The One who knew her past was the One she had been waiting for.
She came because she needed water.
She left the thing she came to fill.
Then she went into the city.
“Come meet a man who thinks I'm amazing.”
“Come meet someone who affirmed every decision I've ever made.”
“Come hear a teacher who told me my past doesn't matter.”
“Come, see a man, which told me all things that ever I did: is not this the Christ?” — John 4:29, KJV
The thing that could have become her humiliation became part of her testimony.
and she was still standing there.
and He was leading her toward truth.
and living water was still being offered.
Maybe that is what someone reading this desperately needs to understand tonight.
You are not protecting Him from shocking information.
Your confession will never make an omniscient Christ suddenly discover something about you.
He knows what happened in that room.
He knows why the marriage is hurting.
He knows what was done to you.
He knows what you did to somebody else.
He knows the addiction you renamed a “struggle” because addiction sounded too frightening.
He knows the resentment underneath the smile.
He knows the theology in your mouth and the rebellion hidden in your heart.
And His knowledge is not permission to keep hiding.
It is an invitation to finally stop.
There is an enormous difference between being exposed by people who want to destroy you and being brought into truth by Christ who calls sinners to repentance and gives eternal life.
Jesus does not save us by pretending sin isn't sin.
Jesus discovered you were actually innocent.
The Gospel is that we are sinners who cannot rescue ourselves, and the Son of God came to save.
Forgiveness is not purchased by our religious performance, our reputation, our tears, our charitable giving, or our ability to reinvent ourselves.
Repentance means we stop negotiating with the darkness and turn toward Him.
Grace means the sinner who deserves judgment can receive mercy because of Christ.
And transformation means Jesus doesn't merely forgive where we've been.
He becomes Lord over where we're going.
At the beginning, she was talking to Jesus alone at a well.
Later, she was telling a city about Him.
John tells us that many Samaritans from that city believed in Jesus because of the woman's testimony.
The woman whose complicated history could have silenced her became a witness pointing others toward Christ.
Not “look how clean my history is.”
The Savior knows what I could never hide.
And after the Samaritans encountered Him themselves, they confessed that He truly is “the Christ, the Saviour of the world.”
This story was never ultimately about a scandalous woman.
It was about a glorious Savior.
Maybe that's why you're still reading.
Maybe somewhere between her well and your screen, the story stopped feeling ancient.
Maybe you realized you have been thirsty too.
Your own sentence you don't want Jesus to finish.
And perhaps you have spent years believing that if Christ really saw everything, He would want nothing to do with you.
But the Samaritan woman teaches us something astonishing.
Being completely known by Jesus and being invited to receive His living water can exist in the same conversation.
Grace is not God failing to notice your sin.
Grace is God knowing the truth and providing the Savior you desperately need.
Not because He needs the information.
Lay down the relationship you know dishonors Him.
Forgive the person whose name still changes your heartbeat.
Ask forgiveness where you have wounded someone.
Stop feeding what is killing your spiritual hunger.
And when shame whispers, “If people knew everything about you, they would never look at you the same,” remember the Savior at the well.
He knew before the conversation started.
If this exposed something you've been hiding, don't turn the comment section into another place to pretend.
You don't need to publish private details. You don't owe strangers your wounds.
Your testimony may become somebody else's invitation to come and see.
But never confuse supporting a ministry with purchasing God's favor.
You cannot share enough Christian posts to earn forgiveness.
Supporting Gospel work should flow from gratitude and love for God—not fear, pressure, or an attempt to purchase His blessing.
And don't keep Gospel Warrior to yourself.
Invite the friend who has drifted from church.
Invite the believer who is exhausted.
Invite the person asking difficult questions about Christianity.
Invite the lukewarm Christian who needs truth more than another motivational quote.
Even invite the unbelieving friend who may not agree with us yet.
And Jesus in front of her.
She thought the deepest fact about her life might be what she had done, what had happened to her, whom she had loved, whom she had lost, or how complicated her story had become.
The deepest fact was that the Messiah had come near.
Maybe there are chapters you would burn if you could.
Maybe people remember you by your worst season.
Maybe you remember yourself that way.
But when Jesus Christ becomes the center of the story, your scandal does not get the final word.
Not grace that baptizes rebellion and calls it freedom.
The grace that tells the truth…
and turns wounded, thirsty people into witnesses who can say:
Because the most unforgettable thing about the woman at the well was never that she had five husbands.
It was that Jesus knew the whole story—and still came to the well.
